identification.summary: China-based cyberespionage group that Microsoft tracks as Brocade Typhoon (formerly BORON) and that other vendors call APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS, Buckeye and TG-0110 [S1][S4]. FireEye/Mandiant tied it to browser and Flash zero-day campaigns in 2014-2015 (Operation Clandestine Fox, Operation Clandestine Wolf) [S2][S9]. Symantec reported a targeting shift from the US to Hong Kong political entities starting in June 2015 [S4]. Security researchers linked the group to the Guangzhou firm Boyusec, three of whose personnel were indicted by the US in November 2017 [S6][S7]. Symantec reported that known Buckeye tool activity ceased in mid-2017 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec (2016) assessed the group had been operating for 'well over half a decade' [S4]; the 2017 US indictment alleges intrusions from 2011 to May 2017 (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Earliest named public campaign: Operation Clandestine Fox, April 2014 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Brocade Typhoon. Microsoft's public mapping lists BORON, GOTHIC PANDA, UPS, APT3, OLDCARP, TG-0110, Red Sylvan and CYBRAN as other names [S1]. Symantec calls it Buckeye and equates it with APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS Team and TG-0110 [S4]. Palo Alto Unit 42 tracks the same activity as UPS and associates it with the Pirpi backdoor [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as APT3 (G0022) [S11]. Boyusec is a company the researchers link to the group; whether Boyusec is all of APT3 or only one component was unresolved in 2017 reporting [S8].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS), per Recorded Future's assessment that Boyusec worked on behalf of the MSS [S6]. The US indictment does not name the Chinese government [S7][S8].
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future assessed with high confidence (May 2017) that APT3 is attributable to the MSS through the contractor Boyusec [S6]. FireEye's Ben Read said FireEye believed the indicted individuals and Boyusec are linked to APT3 [S7]. The November 2017 US indictment charged three Boyusec personnel (Wu Yingzhuo, Dong Hao, Xia Lei) but, per press reporting, made no reference to Chinese state links [S7][S8]. Microsoft's mapping lists the origin as China [S1].
attribution.basis: Domain-registration analysis by the anonymous 'intrusiontruth' blog tied Pirpi C2 domains to Boyusec shareholders, which Recorded Future corroborated and linked to Guangdong ITSEC, which it describes as subordinate to the MSS-run CNITSEC [S6][S8]. Charges against Boyusec personnel cited use of 'UPS'/'exeproxy' malware (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Vendor malware and campaign reporting from FireEye/Mandiant, Symantec and Unit 42 [S2][S3][S4][S5][S10].

objectives: Espionage and theft of commercial and technical intellectual property: the indictment alleges theft of Siemens energy, technology and transportation business data, Trimble satellite-navigation (GNSS) development data and Moody's Analytics economist email (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. From 2015 it also collected against political entities in Hong Kong [S4].

sectors: Industrial and engineering (Siemens energy, technology, transportation businesses) [S7]
regions: Vietnam and the Philippines (later use of the Bemstour/DoublePulsar package; Symantec did not tie that later use to Buckeye's known tools) [S12]
targeting.notes: Symantec counted 13 Hong Kong, 3 US and 1 UK victim organizations in its 2016 reporting, and said US and UK targeting stopped from March 2016 (reported by SecurityWeek) [S4]. The Vietnam and Philippines intrusions used the Bemstour exploit tool with different malware after Buckeye's known tools went quiet in mid-2017, so they may not belong to this cluster [S5][S12].

capabilities.summary: Early access to browser and plugin zero-days: Internet Explorer CVE-2014-1776 (Clandestine Fox, April 2014) [S9] and Adobe Flash CVE-2015-3113 delivered by phishing links to compromised servers, followed by the SHOTPUT backdoor (Clandestine Wolf, June 2015) [S2]. Rapid use of newly disclosed exploits such as CVE-2014-6332 and CVE-2014-4113 within days of disclosure (Operation Double Tap, November 2014), with PlugX/Kaba C2 noted [S3]. Custom backdoors including Pirpi/UPS [S10] and 'exeproxy' [S7]. From March 2016 the group used a DoublePulsar variant, newer than the Shadow Brokers version, delivered by the custom Bemstour exploit tool, which chained Windows vulnerabilities including the zero-day CVE-2019-0703 for remote kernel code execution; this was over a year before the Shadow Brokers leak [S5]. Spearphishing with malicious attachments or links is alleged in the indictment [S7]. MITRE lists software including PlugX, SHOTPUT, OSInfo, RemoteCMD and LaZagne [S11].

campaigns.name: Intrusions charged in US indictment (Boyusec)
campaigns.summary: Alleged intrusions into Moody's Analytics, Siemens and Trimble between 2011 and May 2017, including theft of 407 GB of Siemens data in 2014 and Trimble GNSS data in 2015-2016.

campaigns.name: Operation Clandestine Fox
campaigns.summary: FireEye reports targeted attacks exploiting Internet Explorer zero-day CVE-2014-1776 against IE9-IE11 by an APT group with access to browser zero-days.

campaigns.name: Operation Double Tap
campaigns.summary: Spearphishing campaign beginning 2014-11-19 using recently disclosed CVE-2014-6332 and CVE-2014-4113; Mandiant noted a shift away from zero-days.

campaigns.name: Operation Clandestine Wolf
campaigns.summary: Phishing campaign exploiting Adobe Flash zero-day CVE-2015-3113 to install the SHOTPUT backdoor; Adobe released an out-of-band patch on 23 June 2015.

campaigns.name: Hong Kong targeting shift
campaigns.summary: Symantec reports Buckeye began compromising Hong Kong political entities from June 2015 and focused mostly on Hong Kong from March 2016.

campaigns.name: Bemstour / DoublePulsar use
campaigns.summary: Earliest known Buckeye use of a DoublePulsar variant (31 March 2016, Hong Kong target), delivered via Bemstour, more than a year before the Shadow Brokers leak.

campaigns.name: Public attribution to MSS via Boyusec
campaigns.summary: intrusiontruth blog links Pirpi infrastructure to Boyusec; Recorded Future assesses with high confidence that the MSS is behind APT3.

campaigns.name: US indictment unsealed
campaigns.summary: Charges against Wu Yingzhuo, Dong Hao and Xia Lei of Boyusec unsealed in Pittsburgh; known Buckeye tool activity had ceased by mid-2017.

diamond.adversary: PRC-based operators linked by researchers to Guangzhou Boyu Information Technology (Boyusec), assessed by Recorded Future as working for the MSS; three Boyusec personnel indicted by the US [S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Browser and Flash zero-days (CVE-2014-1776, CVE-2015-3113), fast use of new n-days, SHOTPUT, Pirpi/UPS, exeproxy, PlugX, and a pre-leak DoublePulsar variant with Bemstour (CVE-2019-0703) [S2][S3][S5][S7][S9][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Phishing links to compromised servers hosting exploits [S2]; actor-registered C2 domains, including Pirpi domains registered to a Boyusec shareholder [S6][S8]; domains such as securitywap.com and walterclean.com in Double Tap [S3]; email forwarding rules on a victim mail server [S7].
diamond.victim: US aerospace, defense and industrial firms (Siemens, Trimble, Moody's Analytics); Hong Kong political entities; targets in the UK and Belgium [S2][S4][S7][S12].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial and technical IP theft benefiting PRC industrial priorities, plus political intelligence on Hong Kong from 2015 [S4][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Internet Explorer and Adobe Flash; Windows SMB and kernel vulnerabilities exploited by Bemstour; enterprise email servers [S5][S7][S9].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report specific to Brocade Typhoon/BORON was found; Microsoft coverage is limited to its naming map [S1].
The DOJ press release and indictment (justice.gov) could not be opened; indictment details come from Security Affairs and Foreign Policy coverage [S7][S8].

The original FireEye/Mandiant, Symantec, Recorded Future, Unit 42 and Secureworks (BRONZE MAYFAIR) pages could not be fetched (network blocks); details come from search-result summaries and press coverage.
MITRE ATT&CK G0022 could not be fetched in this session; the software list is taken from the imported actor record [S11].

Activity after mid-2017 is not publicly attributed to this cluster. Bemstour/DoublePulsar use into late 2018 (Vietnam, Philippines) was with different malware, and Symantec did not attribute it to Buckeye [S5][S12].
It is unresolved whether Boyusec is the whole of APT3 or one part of it, and how Buckeye obtained Equation Group tools [S5][S8].
Aliases Boyusec, Group 6, Pirpi, Threat Group-0110 and UPS Team in the imported record come from MISP/other mappings; only those in cited sources are added below.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints running browsers and plugins, enterprise mail servers and Windows SMB-exposed hosts at defense, aerospace, industrial and navigation-technology firms, including DIB contractors whose engineering data has value (Siemens, Trimble precedent) [S2][S5][S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Zero-day and fast n-day use (exploits within about a week of disclosure) shortens the defender's patch window; stealthy mail-forwarding rules allow long-term, low-noise collection [S3][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): phishing link or attachment, then browser/Flash exploit, then SHOTPUT/Pirpi/PlugX backdoor, then credential theft and lateral movement, possibly with a kernel-level implant such as DoublePulsar, then data staging and exfiltration [S2][S3][S5][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet theft of engineering and program data (for example GNSS and energy technology) from DIB and partner networks. MDCOA is use of an unpublished exploit chain that gives kernel-level implants across many hosts. Candidate indicators: unexpected mailbox forwarding rules to external accounts, anomalous SMB traffic consistent with DoublePulsar, browser processes spawning shells, and connections to newly registered domains [S5][S7]. Note: no public activity has been attributed since mid-2017 [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track emergency browser, plugin and Windows patches alongside exposure of mission-relevant enclaves, since this actor used exploits within days of disclosure [S3]. (2) Authorities: activity against contractors such as Siemens and Trimble falls under law enforcement and DIB channels; the US addressed it by indictment, not military response [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: PNT-related development data (Trimble GNSS) was a target, so protect PNT program and supplier data as mission-critical [S7]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB CS partners and commercial vendors, since public attribution came from vendor and researcher reporting (Recorded Future, Symantec, FireEye) [S5][S6][S7].
